In [[statistical process control|statistical quality control]], an '''EWMA chart''' (or '''exponentially weighted moving average chart''') is a type of [[control chart]] used to monitor either variables or attributes-type data using the monitored [[Business process|business]] or [[List of industrial processes|industrial process]]'s entire history of output.<REF name="NISTEWMA">{{cite web|url=http://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pmc/section3/pmc324.htm|title=EWMA Control Charts|accessdate=2009-08-10|work=Engineering Statistics Handbook|publisher=[[National Institute of Standards and Technology]]}}</REF>  While other control charts treat rational subgroups of samples individually, the EWMA chart tracks the [[EWMA|exponentially-weighted moving average]] of all prior sample means.  EWMA weights samples in geometrically decreasing order so that the most recent samples are weighted most highly while the most distant samples contribute very little.<REF name="Montgomery2005">
{{cite book | last = Montgomery | first = Douglas | title = Introduction to Statistical Quality Control | publisher = [[John Wiley & Sons]], Inc. | date = 2005 | location = [[Hoboken, New Jersey]] | url = http://www.eas.asu.edu/~masmlab/montgomery/ | isbn = 978-0-471-65631-9 | oclc = 56729567 | access-date = 2009-08-10 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080620095346/http://www.eas.asu.edu/~masmlab/montgomery/ | archive-date = 2008-06-20 | url-status = dead }}
</REF>{{rp|406}}

Although the [[normal distribution]] is the basis of the EWMA chart, the chart is also relatively robust in the face of [[Normal distribution|non-normally distributed]] quality characteristics.<REF name="Montgomery2005"/>{{rp|412}} There is, however, an adaptation of the chart that accounts for quality characteristics that are better modeled by the [[Poisson distribution]].<REF name="Montgomery2005"/>{{rp|415}} The chart monitors only the process mean; monitoring the process variability requires the use of some other technique.<REF name = "Montgomery2005"/>{{rp|414}}

The EWMA control chart requires a knowledgeable person to select two parameters before setup:
#The first parameter is λ, the weight given to the most recent rational subgroup mean.  λ must satisfy 0 < λ ≤ 1, but selecting the "right" value is a matter of personal preference and experience.  One 2005 textbook recommends 0.05 ≤ λ ≤ 0.25,<REF name="Montgomery2005"/>{{rp|411}} while a 1986 journal article recommends 0.1 ≤ λ ≤ 0.3.<ref>J. S. Hunter, The Exponentially Weighted Moving Average, ''Journal of Quality Technology'' 18: 203-210, 1986. {{doi|10.1080/00224065.1986.11979014}}</ref>
#The second parameter is L, the multiple of the rational subgroup standard deviation that establishes the control limits.  L is typically set at 3 to match other control charts, but it may be necessary to reduce L slightly for small values of λ.<REF name="Montgomery2005"/>{{rp|406}}

Instead of plotting rational subgroup averages directly, the EWMA chart computes successive observations z<SUB>i</SUB> by computing the rational subgroup average, <math>\bar x_i</math>, and then combining that new subgroup average with the running average of all preceding observations, z<SUB>i - 1</SUB>, using the specially–chosen weight, λ, as follows:
:<math>z_i = \lambda \bar x_i + \left ( 1 - \lambda \right)z_{i - 1}</math>.

The control limits for this chart type are <math>T \pm L\frac {S}{\sqrt n}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{2 - \lambda}\lbrack 1 - \left ( 1 - \lambda \right )^{2i} \rbrack}</math> where T and S are the estimates of the long-term process mean and standard deviation established during control-chart setup and n is the number of samples in the rational subgroup.  Note that the limits widen for each successive rational subgroup, approaching <math>\pm L\frac {\hat \sigma}{\sqrt n}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{2-\lambda}}</math>.<REF name="Montgomery2005"/>{{rp|407}}

The EWMA chart is sensitive to small shifts in the process mean, but does not match the ability of Shewhart-style charts (namely the [[Xbar and R chart|<math>\bar x</math> and R]] and [[Xbar and s chart|<math>\bar x</math> and s chart]]s) to detect larger shifts.<REF name="Montgomery2005"/>{{rp|412}} One author recommends superimposing the EWMA chart on top of a suitable Shewhart-style chart with widened control limits in order to detect both small and large shifts in the process mean.{{citation needed|date=April 2010}}

Exponentially weighted moving variance (EWMVar) can be used to obtain a significance score or limits that automatically adjust to the observed data.<ref>{{Cite conference | doi = 10.1145/2623330.2623740| title = SigniTrend: scalable detection of emerging topics in textual streams by hashed significance thresholds| conference = Proceedings of the 20th ACM SIGKDD international conference on Knowledge discovery and data mining - KDD '14| pages = 871–880| year = 2014| last1 = Schubert | first1 = E. | last2 = Weiler | first2 = M. | last3 = Kriegel | first3 = H. P. | authorlink3 = Hans-Peter Kriegel| isbn = 9781450329569}}</ref><ref>Finch, Tony. (2009). ''Incremental calculation of weighted mean and variance.'' [https://fanf2.user.srcf.net/hermes/doc/antiforgery/stats.pdf PDF]. University of Cambridge Computing Service.</ref>
